newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: BASEBALL-BUDSKY BECOMES FIRST CZECH NATIONAL TO WIN CONTRACT.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-BUDSKY BECOMES FIRST CZECH NATIONAL TO WIN CONTRACT.

text.p: World javelin record holder Jan Zelezny briefly captured the baseball world's attention after winning the Olympic title this year when he threw a ball across the field and out of the stadium during a training session with the Atlanta Braves.

Zelezny's appearance was more of a gimmick than a serious attempt to try out for a baseball career and it is his 22-year-old compatriot Pavel Budsky who will be the first Czech national to sign with a major league team.
Budsky has signed a one-year contract with the Montreal Expos and is likely to begin next season in the Expos' farm system.

"I'm aware that a pretty difficult job is in front of me but I have the ambition to get to the major leagues," Budsky said after returning from the Expos' camp in Florida. "And as far as I can observe the situation in America, I think I'm capable of reaching that."
Unlike Zelezny, who has never played baseball in his life, Budsky has 10 years' experience.
"Baseball was always my hobby, I can hardly believe it's going to be my job. I will be playing on behalf of the whole country so I don't want to disappoint."
Baseball in Czechoslovakia dates back to World War Two when American troops helped liberate the country and sparked enduring interest in the U.S. national summer sport.
During the communist era the game was kept alive mainly by young Cubans who came to the country as part of a student exchange system.

If Budsky does make the Expos' big league roster, he will become the fifth Czech-born player to take part in the major leagues. The other four were immigrants who learned the sport after arriving in the United States.

Budsky's path to the Expos began in 1988 when Jerry Stitt, coach at the University of Arizona, flew to Czechoslovakia to help direct a baseball clinic. Stitt spotted the young Budsky and was impressed with his ability.
Five years after the fall of communism in 1989, Stitt returned to Prague and to Budksy who was playing with the Czech national team.
"He was the best player in the Czech republic," Stitt said.

Budsky travelled to Arizona in the spring of 1995 to work out with the university team and caught the eye of Scott Stanley, a scout with the Expos. Stanley was immediately impressed with the size and strength of Budsky who stands 1.98 metres tall and weighs 98 kg.

"He's a big, strong kid and that partially makes up for his lack of experience playing the game at a high level," he said. Stanley urged the Expos' management to invite Budsky to a training camp in Florida in October.
Budsky took a gamble, travelling back to the United States at his own expense, a move which has paid off .
"They see him as first baseman and as a hitter with good power potential," Stanley said. "He showed good power down in Fort Lauderdale."

Stanley predicted after spring training, Budsky would probably be assisgned to the Expos' lower level farm teams, but added Montreal, a team known for developing its prospects, was patient with youngsters such as Budsky.
"I would say it will take two years of playing to learn to deal with breaking balls and the velocity he will be seeing regularly," Stanley said.
"But the Expos don't just bring in a kid for one year. We sign a player, bring him in and give him a fair chance to develop."
